strengths: Automatically generating image-specific segmentation vocabularies addresses a useful practical problem. AutoSeg reuses pretrained models without additional model training.

Decoding localized subsets of BLIP embeddings is a plausible technical contribution. Table 1 supports its usefulness: BBoost guidance improves class-agnostic IoU over BLIP plus X-Decoder on all four datasets.

The experiments cover diverse datasets and several alternative pipelines. Table 3 reports substantial improvements over LLaVA plus X-Decoder on VOC (87.1 versus 56.7 mIoU) and Cityscapes (30.0 versus 23.4).

LAVE addresses a real evaluation difficulty, and its results are within 1.1 mIoU points of the manual mappings across all four datasets. Clear pipeline illustrations, mapping pseudocode, citations to underlying models and datasets, and explicit failure examples aid understanding.
weaknesses: LAVE is insufficiently validated as an evaluation protocol. Section 9.3 relies on the LLM remembering the PASCAL Context and ADE20K vocabularies rather than supplying their class lists. Its prompts also direct stuff categories to background, potentially rejecting valid stuff synonyms in datasets that annotate them. Small aggregate differences from manual mapping do not establish mapping accuracy or robustness to prompts and model choice.

The comparison with ZeroSeg does not establish equivalent supervision and evaluation conditions. AutoSeg uses a pretrained segmentation model, whereas ZeroSeg targets zero segment labels; a common label mapper is not documented. Table A7 shows that changing only the mapper changes VOC scores by 9.6–13.2 points. These confounds particularly weaken the interpretation of the 0.3-point PASCAL Context advantage.

Model selection and stochastic uncertainty are unclear. Section 5.1 describes Bayesian optimization against VOC mIoU without identifying a separate tuning split. Tables 3–4 report the best caption-cycle setting for each dataset from Table 2, but independent selection data are not specified. Repeated-run variability is absent despite stochastic clustering and caption generation.

The central claim of accurate open-ended recognition has limited direct quantitative support. Mapping predictions back to fixed categories cannot verify finer distinctions such as breed or role, and producing more unique nouns does not establish correctness or coverage. A representative assessment of generated labels and hallucination frequency would strengthen this claim beyond selected qualitative examples.

The task-level novelty is overstated because the cited ZeroSeg already performs segmentation without supplied category names. The original contribution should be positioned around BBoost and its evaluation approach, rather than introducing automatic-vocabulary segmentation itself.

Secondary reproducibility issues require clarification: Equation 9 specifies independent maximum-IoU assignments despite describing Hungarian matching, cross-resolution cluster alignment is underspecified, and Table A6 reports 87.1 VOC mIoU with one captioning cycle whereas Table 2 reports 85.3. Runtime measurements are also missing for the repeated clustering and captioning pipeline. These issues are less consequential than the evaluation concerns above.
